clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder of galactose metabolism; the classic and most severe form results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT).
Symptoms typically begin in the first days to weeks of life once milk feeding (which contains lactose, a source of galactose) is established.
Presenting features include poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and lethargy, often progressing to liver dysfunction and coagulopathy.
Affected neonates are at markedly increased risk of Escherichia coli sepsis, which may be the presenting or dominant feature.
Cataracts can develop early owing to accumulation of galactitol in the lens.
Diagnosis is supported by newborn screening and confirmed by demonstrating reduced GALT enzyme activity and characteristic metabolite abnormalities; a reducing substance may be found in the urine.
The cornerstone of management is strict, lifelong elimination of galactose and lactose from the diet, which reverses the acute toxicity.
Despite early dietary treatment, long-term complications such as speech and cognitive difficulties, ataxia, and ovarian insufficiency in females may still occur.
Milder variant forms (for example some Duarte variants) may have residual enzyme activity and a more benign course.
reference.pathophysiology: Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase blocks the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose in the Leloir pathway. Ingested galactose, mainly from lactose in milk, cannot be normally metabolised, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in tissues including the liver, kidney, and brain and exerts toxic effects. Excess galactose is also shunted to alternative pathways, generating galactitol, which accumulates in the lens and causes cataract, and galactonate. The metabolite toxicity produces hepatocellular injury, renal tubular dysfunction, and central nervous system effects, and impairs host defences, predisposing to Gram-negative sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neonatal cholestasis and liver failure
Tyrosinemia and other hepatorenal metabolic disorders
Urea cycle disorders presenting with encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Newborn screening result and confirmatory GALT enzyme activity assay
Quantitative galactose-1-phosphate and molecular genetic testing
Liver function tests and coagulation studies
Urine for reducing substances (a supportive, non-specific finding)
Blood cultures and sepsis evaluation given the risk of E. coli infection
redFlags: Signs of Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative sepsis in a jaundiced neonate
Acute liver failure with coagulopathy and bleeding
Progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and encephalopathy
Continued galactose exposure delaying recognition and worsening toxicity
reference.prognosis: Early diagnosis and strict dietary galactose restriction reverse the life-threatening acute manifestations. However, even with good control, a substantial proportion of children experience long-term neurodevelopmental, speech, and motor difficulties, and most affected females develop primary ovarian insufficiency. Variant forms are generally milder.
pitfalls: Treating neonatal sepsis without considering an underlying metabolic disorder such as galactosemia
Delaying dietary galactose elimination while awaiting confirmatory results in a decompensating infant
Assuming that early dietary treatment fully prevents all long-term complications
Overlooking milder variants that may still need dietary attention
Failing to arrange ophthalmological and developmental follow-up
